sections.body:
Rain is not new water. It is old water that has taken a long trip around.

All the water on Earth sits in a few places. It is in the sea, in rivers, in lakes, in the soil, and in you. The Sun warms it, and warm water rises into the air as vapour. Vapour is water in its invisible gas form.

High above the ground the air is cold. Cold air cannot hold as much vapour as warm air. So the vapour turns back into tiny drops of water. Millions of these drops together make a cloud.

When the drops grow heavy enough, they fall. That is rain.

The water lands on the ground, runs into rivers and the sea, and the whole trip starts again. Scientists call this round trip the water cycle.

The same water has been falling as rain for billions of years. The glass of water at your table once fell as rain on a dinosaur.

Rain is the sky giving the water back.
examples: Rain is old water that has been round the cycle many times.
The Sun warms the water and lifts it into the air.
That glass of water was rain a very long time ago.
sections.heading: Where rain comes from

sections.body:
The Sun is the engine of the whole thing. Its warmth pushes water at the surface into the air.

You can watch this with a saucer of water on a sunny windowsill. After a few hours, the saucer is dry. The water did not vanish. It turned into vapour and drifted away.

Warm vapour rises because warm air is lighter than cold air. It climbs higher and higher, and on the way it cools down.

Salt does not go up with it. When the vapour comes back down as rain, it is fresh water, even the rain that falls on the sea.

Plants help too. Their leaves let out water vapour through tiny holes. A big tree can put out a lot of water on a hot day. This is why forests often have their own small clouds above them.
examples: The water on the saucer turned into vapour and floated away.
Warm vapour rises because warm air is lighter.
Rain that falls on the sea is fresh water, not salty.
sections.heading: How water rises into the sky

sections.body:
A raindrop can start anywhere. Follow one and you will see the whole cycle.

It starts as water in a puddle, a river, or the sea. Then it has to travel a long way through the air before it becomes a drop of rain again.
examples: The sun warmed the puddle, and the water went up as vapour.
The tiny drops joined together until the cloud was grey.
Then the rain came down and the journey started over.
sections.heading: How one raindrop travels
steps: The Sun warms the water and it turns into vapour.
The warm vapour rises high into the sky.
Cold air makes the vapour turn back into tiny drops.
The drops join together and grow heavy.
They fall as rain, and the water starts again.

sections.body: Not all wet weather is the same. Drizzle is rain with drops so small they hang in the air. Rain has bigger drops and falls faster. Snow is water that froze into ice crystals high in the cold air, so it falls as soft white flakes. Hail is ice that grows inside a storm cloud, where strong updraughts keep throwing it up until it is too heavy to stay, and then it falls as little balls of ice.
sections.heading: Rain, drizzle, snow and hail

sections.body:
These four words are the heart of the water cycle.

Evaporation is when liquid water turns into vapour and rises into the air.

Condensation is when vapour cools and turns back into tiny drops of water. This is how a cloud is made.

A **cloud** is a big group of those tiny drops, or of ice crystals, floating in the air.

Precipitation is any water that falls out of a cloud. Rain is precipitation. Snow and hail are precipitation too.
examples: Evaporation is water going up into the air.
Condensation is water turning back into drops.
Precipitation means water falling out of a cloud.
sections.heading: The words we use for water in the sky

terms.example: Evaporation dried the wet clothes on the line.
terms.gloss: When liquid water warms up, turns into vapour, and rises into the air.

terms.example: Condensation makes the cloud in the sky.
terms.gloss: When vapour cools and turns back into tiny drops of water, like the drops on a cold glass.

terms.example: That cloud is grey because it holds so much water.
terms.gloss: A huge group of tiny water drops, or ice crystals, floating together high in the air.

terms.example: The forecast said precipitation, so I took my umbrella.
terms.gloss: Any water that falls out of a cloud: rain, snow, sleet or hail.

sections.body:
Rain does not fall as a fine mist. It falls in drops, and here is why.

As the drops swirl around inside a cloud, they bump into each other and join. Bigger drops are heavier, so they fall faster. They fall faster, so they sweep up more small drops on the way. The drops keep growing until the air cannot hold them up any more.

Then they fall out of the bottom of the cloud. A drop that starts small and grows big takes about ten minutes to reach the ground.

The size of the drop decides how heavy the rain feels. Small drops make a light drizzle. Big drops make a heavy shower that drums on the window.

Rain can also freeze on the way down and arrive as ice. That is why some showers are called sleet.
examples: The drops joined together inside the cloud until they were heavy.
Heavy rain drums loudly on the window.
Sleet is rain that froze on the way down.
sections.heading: Why rain falls in drops

item.summary: Rain is old water that has taken a long trip. Water from rivers, lakes and puddles rises into the air, cools, gathers into clouds, and falls back down as drops. After reading this you can explain where rain comes from, name the three steps of the water cycle, and tell the difference between rain, drizzle, snow and hail.
item.title: Where Does Rain Come From?
